claims.text: Catastrophic failure during elevated-temperature exposure originates from rapid formation of an interconnected intergranular oxide network.
Selective oxidation of Ti and Al at grain boundaries drives formation of the interconnected oxide network.
The intergranular oxide network embrittles the fcc matrix.
The oxide network concentrates stress and nucleates cracks that coalesce during thermal cycling.
The as-built alloy has a single-phase fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy has no pre-existing oxide scale.
The as-built alloy has equiaxed grains approximately 50 µm in size.
Reducing Ti from the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 composition to Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.2 while holding other formula coefficients and AM processing constant is the proposed controlled intervention.
Lower Ti content slows nucleation and growth of Ti-rich oxides at grain boundaries.
Slower Ti-rich oxide formation prevents development of a continuous brittle intergranular oxide network.
Preventing the continuous oxide network reduces embrittlement and crack initiation.
After the specified exposure and cycling, the Ti-reduced alloy will have at least 30% thinner intergranular oxide films than the baseline alloy.
After the specified exposure and cycling, the Ti-reduced alloy will have at least 50% fewer grain-boundary cracks than the baseline alloy.
The original alloy after identical exposure has a continuous intergranular oxide network approximately 2 µm thick.
The original alloy after identical exposure has an average crack density of approximately 10 cracks/mm.
The proposed mechanism applies from 600–800 °C, oxygen partial pressures of 0.1–0.21 atm, and exposure times of 10–1000 h.
The proposed mechanism does not address purely reducing environments.

contradictions.description: The Ti values 0.3 and 0.2 are described as atomic percentages, but in the stated formulas they are stoichiometric coefficients. Normalization gives approximately 5.45 at.% Ti for Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 and 3.70 at.% Ti for Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.2, not 0.3 and 0.2 at.%.

The prediction requires at least 30% thinner oxide films and 50% fewer cracks, whereas falsification requires failure to achieve at least 20% reductions in both. Outcomes between these thresholds can fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis, leaving a non-decisive interpretive gap.
